title: Peter Village Enclosure (15Fa166): Early Woodland in Fayette County
summary: Peter Village (15Fa166), an Early Woodland earthwork in Fayette County, has pottery dated to about 409–68 BCE and is a protected site.
bodyMarkdown:
Peter Village is an Early Woodland earthwork in Fayette County, recorded by archaeologists as site 15Fa166. Its builders left no written name for the place. What they left was earth: an enclosure raised by hand, one of the many mounds and earthworks that early Woodland peoples built across the Bluegrass.

Pottery from the site has been dated to about 409–68 BCE. That places Peter Village more than two thousand years before Kentucky's first forts and stations. Its builders lived at the same time as people archaeologists group under the name [Adena culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture). Adena is an archaeologists' name for a shared way of life, not the name of a single tribe. Communities that shared it built burial mounds and circular or walled enclosures, made distinctive stone and copper ornaments, and traded across the Ohio Valley.

Why build an enclosure at all? Archaeologists still debate the answer. Some earthworks seem to have been gathering places, where scattered families met for ceremonies, trade, burials, and feasts. Others may have marked boundaries or sacred ground. A large enclosure meant many people working together over seasons, which tells us these communities could organize far beyond a single household.

Peter Village drew attention early. Ephraim Squier and Edwin Davis published a plan of it in their 1848 survey, *Ancient Monuments of the Mississippi Valley*, one of the first attempts to map the earthworks of the eastern United States. Their book recorded many sites that farming and building later damaged or erased.

Peter Village and other Bluegrass earthworks show that this region was a landscape of gathering places long before it was a landscape of farms and towns.

## Kentucky today

Peter Village is a protected archaeological site, so this site names it but does not map it; the pin is withheld or rounded. Digging or collecting at archaeological sites without permission is a crime in Kentucky. Ask before you visit any site on private land.
Source: [Adena culture (Grokipedia)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture)
